lessons.title: Fraction sums and decimal patterns

lessons.objective: Predict a recurring decimal, add and subtract fractions and check an estimate.
lessons.before: Reduce the fraction fully before looking at the denominator.

A fraction in lowest terms terminates in base ten if its denominator has no prime factors except 2 and 5.

Use a common denominator, then add or subtract the numerators. Whole and fractional parts can be written as improper fractions.

Estimate the size and sign before calculating. Perform a bracketed difference before the outside sum.

examples.title: Predict a decimal pattern
examples.question:
Think about the fraction \(\frac{1201}{240}\).

  1. Choose what its decimal does. Options: A. Terminates. B. Is irrational. C. Cannot be written as a decimal. D. Recurs.

    [2]

  2. Give evidence from the prime factors of the reduced denominator.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The numerator is one more than a multiple of 240, so the fraction is already in lowest terms.

A factor of 3 remains in the denominator.

Recurs

(b) A power of ten consists entirely of 2s and 5s.

It has a factor of 3.

examples.title: Add two amounts exactly
examples.question:
A workshop uses \(5\frac{1}{2}\) m of ribbon, then \(\frac{4}{3}\) m.

  1. Find the total length in metres.

    [2]

  2. Say which two consecutive whole metres the total is between, or state the whole number if exact.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Use sixths. The terms become \(\frac{33}{6}\) and \(\frac{8}{6}\).

Add the numerators and keep the denominator 6.

\(\frac{41}{6}\)

(b) Compare the numerator of the total with successive multiples of its denominator.

Between 6 and 7 metres.

examples.title: Subtract before adding the next term
examples.question:
A calculation is \(\frac{5}{2}+(\frac{5}{2}-2)\).

  1. Give its exact value.

    [2]

  2. Write the fraction in lowest terms.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Put the two bracket terms over 6. The difference is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Add \(\frac{5}{2}\) to this difference.

\(3\)

(b) Cancel any common factor in numerator and denominator.

\(3\)

lessons.title: Fraction and decimal products and quotients
lessons.summary: Choose accurate written methods and estimate to catch place-value or inverse errors.
lessons.objective: Choose accurate written methods and estimate to catch place-value or inverse errors.
lessons.before: Write the numerator and denominator as products before multiplying.

Cancel common factors before multiplying fractions. A product of two fractions less than 1 is smaller than each positive factor.

Divide by a non-zero fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal.

If both factors have one decimal place, multiply the tenths as integers and divide the product by 100.

Multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten. The quotient stays the same.

examples.title: Cancel before multiplying
examples.question:
Work with \(2\) and \(\frac{3}{5}\).

  1. Find their product exactly.

    [2]

  2. Show how to check whether the product is less than 1.

    [1]

(a) The calculation equals \(\frac{6}{3}\times\frac{3}{5}\).

The equal middle factors cancel.

\(\frac{6}{5}\)

(b) In the form \(\frac{6}{5}\), the comparison is between 6 and 5.

Compare its numerator with its denominator.

examples.title: Divide by a fractional portion
examples.question:
A measurement is \(3\) litres. One unit portion is \(\frac{3}{4}\) litres.

  1. Find how many portions the measurement represents. A fractional answer is allowed.

    [2]

  2. State what the number means.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The calculation is \(3\) divided by \(\frac{3}{4}\).

Multiply by the reciprocal \(\frac{4}{3}\).

\(4\)

(b) A ratio of two lengths, masses or volumes in the same units has no unit.

It is the number of portions, including any final part of a portion.

examples.title: Multiply the decimals
examples.question:
A strip is 7 m long and 3 m wide.

  1. Give the area in square metres.

    [2]

  2. Use rounded lengths to estimate the area.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Work out 70 × 30 = 2100.

Both lengths were multiplied by 10 for that whole-number calculation. Now divide by 100.

\(21\)

(b) 7 is close to 7 and 3 is close to 3.

examples.title: Divide by a decimal
examples.question:
A roll of tape has length 5.44 m. A standard piece is 3.4 m.

  1. Find the length of the roll divided by the standard length.

    [2]

  2. Check by multiplication.

    [1]

(a) To remove the decimal in the divisor, multiply both values by 10.

\(54.4\div 34=1.6\).

\(\frac{8}{5}\)

(b) Multiplication reverses the division.

\(3.4\times1.6=5.44\)

  1. Give its exact value.

    [2]

A club account begins at 300 credits. It gains 5% each round for two rounds.

  1. Find the final total.

lessons.title: Ratio and direct or inverse proportion
lessons.summary: Share in a ratio and decide whether a fixed unit rate or a fixed product applies.
lessons.objective: Share in a ratio and decide whether a fixed unit rate or a fixed product applies.
lessons.before: Use one bar which contains all the parts stated in the ratio.
lessons.ideas:
For a ratio of 2 to 3, there are five equal parts. Divide the total by five to find one part.

In direct proportion, multiplying one quantity by a factor multiplies the other by the same factor.

In inverse proportion, multiplying one quantity by a factor divides the other by the same factor.

examples.title: Share a total in parts
examples.question:
Red and green counters are in the ratio 5 : 3. There are 24 counters altogether.

  1. Find the number of red counters.

    [2]

  2. State the fraction of counters that are green.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) There are 8 equal parts. Each part contains 3 counters.

Use 5 parts for red.

\(15\)

(b) Green uses 3 parts of the 8 total parts.

\(\frac{3}{8}\)

examples.title: Follow a direct proportion
examples.question:
6 metres of cord cost 9 credits at a constant price per metre.

  1. Find the cost of 11 metres in credits.

    [2]

  2. Describe what doubling the length does to the cost.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) One metre costs 1.5 credits.

Multiply this by 11.

\(\frac{33}{2}\)

(b) The price per metre stays fixed and the length doubles.

It doubles the cost.

examples.title: Use an inverse proportion
examples.question:
14 identical machines complete a run in 18 minutes. They share the work equally and run at the same rate.

  1. Find the time in minutes with 21 machines.

    [2]

  2. Explain how you knew whether the time grows or shrinks.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The fixed amount of work is 14 × 18 machine-minutes.

Share these across 21 machines.

\(12\)

(b) The relationship is an inverse proportion under the stated assumptions.

The total work stays the same. More machines complete it sooner.
